body:
Note: I removed the two lines here (need to confirm):
```
        if messages is None:
            messages = self._oai_messages[sender]
```
Why we can delete this: 
The two lines deleted is in every `generate_<>_reply` function. So when both messages and sender are passed to a subsequent `generate_<>_reply`, it will perform the same logic.
```
final, reply = reply_func(self, messages=messages, sender=sender, config=reply_func_tuple["config"])
``` 

Why needed for compression: Compression will modify `self._oai_messages`, and it is expected that `generate_oai_reply` will use the updated messages from `self._oai_messages`. With the two lines, the messages will not be None and the updated `self._oai_messages` will not be used.

Right, this is complicated. We have below cases:
1. init chat from raguserproxyagent, in this case, the old implementation is fine.
2. init chat from another userproxyagent, we need to address how to update the problem:
2.1. we take the first message raguserproxyagent received as the problem and we keep it. So if raguserproxyagent is selected again, we update the context. (the current implementation in the PR)
2.2. we replace the problem with the current message sent to raguserproxyagent. So we always retrieve docs for the new problem.

Since in a group chat, raguserproxyagent not always talking to ragassistantagent, the original `update context` logic is not valid.

body:
It's a good question. I had three main scenarios in mind:
1. Development and testing, where I would set use_cache=False to see all the effects of non-deterministic LLM generation.
2. Demos for management, where I would set use_cache=True to make the demo run fast and avoid surprises.
3. Production use by customers, who may set it either way depending on their needs.

I've usually been in situation 1, and I assume the same applies to most users of this repo. When starting to write and test this agent, I didn't realize that caching was on by default, which made me waste some time thinking that everything was more stable than it really was.
author: rickyloynd-microsoft

body: Great question! Empirically, it worked better on my tests than giving the instructions only once, whether before or after the text. And conceptually, this is what I expected would happen. The instructions often (but not always) consist of two parts: the description of the analysis, followed by the required format of the response. If the text appears first in the message, then the vector columns that process the text know nothing about the analysis to be performed. But if the analysis tokens come first, then the text vector columns are conditioned directly on the analysis tokens and vector columns, which seems like a more efficient use of transformer computation. But there are also benefits to having the analysis tokens appear for a second time at the end. They give the LLM more tokens to reason over, and force it to revisit the instructions. This is most useful as the text to be analyzed grows in length. Finally, it's important to have any output format requirements at the very end, so they don't get ignored.

Yes, you can control caching via `llm_config`.  I do not have an example from the existing notebooks because we typically want to use cache, which is the default setting. But you can actually do the following to disable caching:

llm_config = {

@LittleLittleCloud I am having trouble understand why this strategy is more robust?

Suggested strategy: one of the agents calls a group chat termination function. user proxy executes. manager detects termination string

author: gagb

body:
> If an agent is smart enough for suggested strategy then it should be able to also do old strategy?

Yes! Unfortunately, that's not the case in the real world, especially for `gpt-3.5-turbo`. For some quite obvious reason I still use `gpt-3.5-turbo` most frequently and `gpt-3.5-turbo` agents are not very robust in generating correct termination messages.

Even for `gpt-4` agents, they might also fail to give the correct termination world when the conversation grows.

The new strategy (using termination_function_call) can make sure the group chat terminate correctly when that termination function_call get triggered. That strategy also works well on gpt-3.5-turbo which fined-tuned for function_call.

body:
If `get_or_create` is False, it means that the user doesn't want to reuse an existing collection. So we'll go into the create function, in which chromadb will try to create the collection and raise an error if a collection with the same name exists. With this setting, users can make sure the collection has the contents given in their running code.

We can remove the existing collection for the users, but that has a high risk if the user doesn't want to remove it. They can just change the collection name.

I suggest we use a new parameter such as `db_action` and send a warning if `get_or_create` is not None, before deprecation, the two are the same.
`db_action` has 3 values: 
- get: Create a collection if it doesn't exist, get the existing collection if it exists.
- recreate: Create a collection if it doesn't exist, remove the existing one and recreate a new one if it exists.
- create: Create a collection if it doesn't exist, raise an error if it exists.

There are two major bugs that arise when using "auto" and allow_repeat_speaker = False. 

First select_speaker_msg ignores the agents param, and populates the agent descriptions from self._participant_roles(), thus including the last_speaker (which may have been excluded in the agents list)

```
    def select_speaker_msg(self, agents: List[Agent]):
        """Return the message for selecting the next speaker."""
        return f"""You are in a role play game. The following roles are available:
{self._participant_roles()}.

Read the following conversation.
Then select the next role from {[agent.name for agent in agents]} to play. Only return the role."""
```

Second, agent_by_name (around L156) will succeed even if it was the last speaker. This can happen due to the above bug, or even when the LLM ignores instructions and just focuses on selecting from the participants in the transcript.
 
Please correct these bugs before merging.

body:
OK, please see a revised section of "Static and dynamic conversations". I had to rewrite the section so that it flows coherently from point to point. Hope it's ok.

#### Static and dynamic conversations

AutoGen, by integrating conversation-driven control utilizing both programming and natural language, inherently supports dynamic conversations. This dynamic nature allows the agent topology to adapt based on the actual conversation flow under varying input problem scenarios. Conversely, static conversations adhere to a predefined topology. Dynamic conversations are particularly beneficial in complex settings where interaction patterns cannot be predetermined.

1. Dynamic Group Chat
The system enables dynamic group chat through a registered auto-reply function. This function allows initiating conversations with other agents based on the current message and context. A practical example is demonstrated in [dynamic group chat](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/notebook/agentchat_groupchat.ipynb) which illustrates the management of dynamic group chats and the decision process for the next speaker.

2. Graph-Based Group Chat
In this approach, a directed graph is fed into [GraphGroupChat](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/notebook/agentchat_two_users.ipynb), an inherited class of `GroupChat`. AutoGen then performs several functions: (1) It seeks a speaker suggestion from the previous speaker, thereby reducing API calls. (2) In the absence of a suggestion, it utilizes the LLM API to nominate the next speaker amongst the eligible speakers. (3) Lastly, it randomly selects from eligible speakers, defined as successor nodes (agents) from the prior speaker (agent). Note that for simpler use cases where all nodes are interconnected, `GroupChat` suffices. However, `GraphGroupChat` is useful for more controlled scenarios requiring specific conversation paths.

3. LLM-Based Function Call
Another approach involves LLM-based function calls, where LLM decides if a specific function should be invoked based on the conversation's status during each inference. This approach enables dynamic multi-agent conversations, as seen in scenarios like [multi-user math problem solving scenario](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/notebook/agentchat_two_users.ipynb), where a student assistant automatically seeks expertise via function calls.

`GraphGroupChat` takes the following steps in sequence to determine the next speaker: (1) It seeks a speaker suggestion from the previous speaker, thereby reducing API calls. (2) If the suggestion from the previous step is not valid, it utilizes the LLM API to nominate the next speaker amongst the eligible speakers. (3) If the suggestion from the previous step is not valid, it randomly selects from eligible speakers, defined as successor nodes (agents) from the prior speaker (agent). A valid suggestion is a transition path that is specified in the directed graph.
```

body:
There are two kinds of accuracy changes we many be concerned about. One is a drop to around 0% accuracy, which would indicate that something is actually broken, like the vector DB. That's the kind of accuracy drop that this test is designed to catch. We also care about a 10% drop in accuracy, but a more complete test set and harness will be required for that. (Issue #537) In short, these tests in test_teachable_agent.py are too few and narrow to detect much beyond a complete failure of teachability.

This particular test will usually complete on the first trial or two. Even if there are 10 trials, the cost in time and $ will be very low, since it uses gpt-3.5. But if we use a maximum of 5 trials, it may assert randomly on 1/500 tests, causing confusion and a waste of time for the people trying to understand the failure. That seems like a high cost. With a max of 10 trials, the chance of a random failure is extremely low.

Currently `AgentBuilder` is also responsible for execution with this `start()` method. Maybe the task building and task execution should be separated? E.g., `AgentBuilder` is resposible for creating the agent and task configurations, as you have here; `AgentExecutor` class is resposible for executing the task with the agents. 

Benefits of separating this two: (1) the builder class can be stateless can build multiple tasks without worry about execution state. (2) forces us to think carefully about the agent and task specification, as we might be adding different task execution runtimes e.g., Rust, Go, and .NET for compute intensive tasks.

body:
Hey @sonichi, before I work on the code, can we expand on this point?

1. `allow_repeat_speaker` is currently used as a check against `speaker_order_dict`, without favoring either parameter.
1a. If `allow_repeat_speaker` is True, then, self-loops are allowed in `speaker_order_dict` for any agent.  We do not create any self-loops in `speaker_order_dict`, just validation checks.
1b. If `allow_repeat_speaker` is a list of Agents, then, self-loops are allowed only for the named agents in `speaker_order_dict`. We do not create/delete any self-loops in `speaker_order_dict`, just validation checks.
1c. If `allow_repeat_speaker` is set to False, then, no self-loops are allowed in `speaker_order_dict` for all agents. Similarly, we do not delete any self-loops present in `speaker_order_dict` but simply raise an error.
1d. These validations are done in `graph_utils.check_graph_validity`. 

2. I would recommend for `allow_repeat_speaker` **not** to be ignored because I think that favoring one parameter as ground-truth (`speaker_order_dict`) and ignoring another parameter (`allow_repeat_speaker`) when both are supplied causes silent failures/ surprises to the user. Extending this principle, I would also not recommend favoring `allow_repeat_speaker` over `speaker_order_dict` by editing `speaker_order_dict` to fit `allow_repeat_speaker`.
2a. FYI `allow_repeat_speaker` is currently defaulted to True in the initialization of `GroupChat`. `allow_repeat_speaker: Optional[Union[bool, List[Agent]]] = True`. I am not sure of the impact of setting `allow_repeat_speaker` to None for now. 
4. I think you are refering to L86-90 of `groupchat.py` instead of `graph_utils.py`. L86-90 is to create the `allowed_speaker_order` so that the rest of the code work with the **whitelist**. I am assuming that all allowed or disallowed self-loops are supplied in `allowed_or_disallowed_speaker_order` (old name `speaker_order_dict`) by the user, and therefore, not considering `allow_repeat_speaker` in L86-90 and only consider it in L93 where `graph_utils.check_graph_validity` is called.

Curious to hear your thoughts on whether any changes is required. :)
author: joshkyh

body:
I don't mean make it a silent failure. We can explicitly raise an error when both of them are provided. For users they don't really need to provide both. In fact, I view "allow_repeat_speaker" as a shortcut to specify a special graph. `speaker_order_dict` is a more general way to specify a graph. They shouldn't be used together. For devs, that simplifies things too. 
Currently allow_repeat_speaker is set to True by default. We can use a `Sentinel` like #831 to handle this problem. If `speaker_order_dict` is not given, then its default is True; otherwise, its default is None.

body:
To answer the question why this test is needed: The main selling point for `register_reply` is the ability to use composition instead of inheritance to define agents. Example use case? An agent that is able to both manage a group chat and reply to external agents. The SocietyOfMind agent is probably the same goal but implemented in a different way. With composition it's possible to simplify the implementation using a single agent. While it's OK to have subclasses of agents under contrib/, we ultimately want to avoid the need of creating a subclass of agents for each commonly desired capability.
This design principle originates from discussion with @ekzhu
author: sonichi

body:
I think that is a reasonable goal, but GroupChatManager *is* a subclass, and the handlers are member functions. All our examples show it being achieved by using this subclass. And we were all confused by this when we saw it.

I think if we want GroupChat to be achieved via composition, there should be no GroupChatManager class, and we should move all examples to achieving the behavior with composition. Otherwise, we end up in this very confusing and mostly undocumented situation.

We should also apply the design principle to RAG, and all the contrib agents which are all based on subclassing (with the notable exception of Teachable Agent with the new PR, but it uses a *different* composition strategy.
author: afourney

body:
All the contrib agents are temporary.
When we put GroupChatManager in the library in the beginning, our goal was to provide a built-in agent class that can be used out of the box. There are users who don't need to modify it. It turns out, there are lot of such users. We did not mean to make it the only way to orchestrate multi-agent chat or stop other agents to have the same orchestration capability.
The specialized extensions of it, as examples, are OK to be made under contrib/. So I haven't enforced the same design principle to be used in every new agent in contrib/, with the expectation that these are experimental and need to iterate quickly.
However, every change to the core will need to use more caution and follow a consistent principle. This PR belongs to this category. The same for #1091. It's very important to make sure these PRs are done properly.

Note that having a convenient class to use is not contradictory to the composability design principle. The composability requires a capability to be composable with others. It doesn't prevent convenient classes with certain default configurations to be offered. AssistantAgent, UserProxyAgent, GroupChatManager are all such convenient classes, and their capabilities are transferrable to other agent classes. We ultimately want to avoid the "need" of creating subclasses, not the "right" of creating them.

I agree with the comment about "undocumented". The discussion here can serve as a good source of documentation improvement.
author: sonichi

body: Composing agent is the current design principle for the core and the three classes (Assistant, UserProxy and GroupChatManager) are examples. The current abstraction of composition through register reply function is a start I think we can have more complete design that models group chat well.

body: There're 10 files that use the pattern of `skip if openai or some other dependencies can't` be imported To make an incremental change we can go with adding a support for skip flag, e.g. `pytest test --skip-openai`. 1. Give pytest a global config via `test/conftest.py` ``` py import pytest skip_openai = False def pytest_addoption(parser): parser.addoption("--skip-openai", action="store_true", help="Skip all tests that require openai") @pytest.hookimpl(tryfirst=True) def pytest_configure(config): global skip_openai skip_openai = config.getoption("--skip-openai", False) ``` 2. Extend the skip criteria everywhere there's the import/skip pattern, e.g. `test/test_retrieve_utils.py` ```py import pytest from conftest import skip_openai try: import chromadb from autogen.retrieve_utils import ( split_text_to_chunks, extract_text_from_pdf, split_files_to_chunks, get_files_from_dir, is_url, create_vector_db_from_dir, query_vector_db, ) from autogen.token_count_utils import count_token except ImportError: skip = True else: skip = False or skip_openai ... ``` _Up until this point tried the changes on 2 files, worked_ 3. Update `build.yaml` ```yaml - name: Test with pytest if: matrix.python-version != '3.10' run: | pytest test --skip-openai ```
author: maxim-saplin

body:
IMO, it makes sense to have a utility function (`getModelForTest(Enum)`) that is a single entry point for all tests requiring OpenAI model interaction. This file will list all models available to tests (as enums). All test that want to make OpenAI calls will got and ask for a model from there.

If a new model is added (e.g. GPT-4 vision) a maintainer would need to got to this model registry file and add the model name there (rather than create own config_list from env, file. etc. which is fragile).

This file can also be a central switchboard determining if a model is available and if not - have OpenAI test skips with the reason 'No XYZ OpenAI model/endpoint is configured'.

This way it is easier to both - (1) run and maintain the tests and (2) make a simple contrib guide

body:
@olaoluwasalami ,

First of all, apologies on the delays in reviewing this (travel).
This looks really good, thanks for all the work put in! 

One thing I'd like us to discuss a bit more (tradeoffs) is that docusaurus 3 seems to require special character escaping not just in the mdx files, but also in the **docstrings used to automatically generate docs**. 

There are some implications/side effects here:

- This pr (which should be purely about the website) seems to touch/modify  many of other files outside of the website (e.g. files in oai completions etc). 
- More importantly, there is now a possibility that changes to the core library can break the website unintentionally. (e.g, if docstrings with non-escaped characters are added the website workflow will break). 
 

@olaoluwasalami (I'd love to hear your thoughts as you have researched this quite a bit) , @skzhang1,  @davorrunje what do you think? 

Some potential approaches we can explore include: 

- research ways to automatically escape characters in the docusarus build without requiring developers to write markdown compliant docstrings. 
- This might involve modifying the build process that converts docstrings to markdown such that special characters are (currently uses pydoc-markdown which seems to be designed for docusaurus v2 and is moving to [novella](https://github.com/NiklasRosenstein/pydoc-markdown/issues/277)) . I can help with investigating this too @olaoluwasalami 

Ideally, it would be great to have a solution where docstring updates do not break the website. 

I realize this is creating more work (apologies), but I would like to discuss this to ensure we are fully aware of the side effects. I still think the move to docusaurus v3 is useful (to enable us take advantage of improved templating).

So, this PR addresses the same issue that was meant to be addressed by the lines 280 - 291 in your code below. Issues #172 and #200 are where they were introduced.

At the time, the warning was added because we wanted to highlight the risk, but not change default behavior due to the installed user base. Perhaps it is now time to change this, and @sonichi can weigh in on this.

But, if we decide now to throw an error, we should remove lines 280-291, and we should update the docstring to mention that the error is thrown, and also update the description of the use_docker field, which now reads:

```
 use_docker (Optional, list, str or bool): The docker image to use for code execution.
            If a list or a str of image name(s) is provided, the code will be executed in a docker container
            with the first image successfully pulled.
            If None, False or empty, the code will be executed in the current environment.
            Default is None, which will be converted into an empty list when docker package is available.
            Expected behaviour:
                - If `use_docker` is explicitly set to True and the docker package is available, the code will run in a Docker container.
                - If `use_docker` is explicitly set to True but the Docker package is missing, an error will be raised.
                - If `use_docker` is not set (i.e., left default to None) and the Docker package is not available, a warning will be displayed, but the code will run natively.
            If the code is executed in the current environment,
            the code must be trusted.
```

And I believe that description is correct (though the language about an "empty" list is confusing)

- More concise and manageable workflows (Which could still use a few edits. I'm about to circle back to it).

body:
If it's an existing pdm project, it's not needed. I assume if the user has an existing pdm project, they will know this. It won't hurt their pyproject.toml even if they run it on an existing pdm project though.

When you run `pdm init` it first looks for things like pyproject.toml, setup.py, and requirements.txt. If a pyproject.toml already exists, it does not delete anything from it. Instead, if it's for instance a poetry project, it will convert the pyproject.toml from poetry to PEP 621. Note: It will not delete the user's existing poetry directives. Example:

```toml
[tool.poetry]
name = "example-project"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "An example Python project."
authors = ["Your Name <you@example.com>"]
license = "MIT"

# Specify the Python versions compatible with your project
[tool.poetry.dependencies]
python = "^3.8"
requests = "^2.25.1"
numpy = "^1.19.4"

# Development dependencies can be specified here
[tool.poetry.dev-dependencies]
pytest = "^6.1.2"

[build-system]
requires = ["poetry-core>=1.0.0"]
build-backend = "poetry.core.masonry.api"
```

becomes:

```toml
[tool.poetry]
name = "example-project"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "An example Python project."
authors = ["Your Name <you@example.com>"]
license = "MIT"

# Specify the Python versions compatible with your project
[tool.poetry.dependencies]
python = ">=3.11,<3.12"

I am sorry, I was not precise enough. My question was not about whether we should use `pdm` as a build system or not, but why don't we install `autogen` in this particular script using `pip`. More precisely, if we replace
```
pdm install -d
```
with
```
pip install -e .
```
below, then we would still use `pdm` backend but through `pip`. Since our users install autogen using `pip`, it would make CI closer to the actual use.

Of course, those two lines should behave the same, but there are always some bugs in both `pip` and `pdm` that could cause different behaviours. In such rare cases, you really want to stick with `pip install` because that way you will catch such bugs in CI.

body:
I think we may want to offer more flexibility when it comes to what types of functions can be registered through this interface. 

For example, right now termination condition is only checked given the message. I often encounter situation when termination is dependent on several other states not limited to:
1. number of messages
2. history of messages
3. who sent the message,
4. etc

So maybe we can add another hierarchy here:
```python
@agent.register_for.termination.on_message() # for checking termination based on message.
@agent.register_for.termination.on_messages() # for checking based on the history. 

# we can add more in the future.
```

In the backend the agent upon receiving a message, it will check all these termination conditions and if any one of them pass it will terminate the conversation -- besides the default termination condition which checks whether the message contains `TERMINATE`

body: IMO the PR is good for what it is - add the ability to tag individual models and filter them using those tags. Yet you touch on a subject of Azure deployment names and indeed it can be anything which creates confusion when you try to map Azure model to a specific OpenAI model (in order to understand token price or context window size). And I don't think that tags alone solve this mapping issues. E.g. if I have a model with deployment name "gpt4x128" as in the screen below, then OAI_CONFIG_LIST will need to have "model" set to "gpt4x128". And this will break cost accounting as there's no such entry in `OAI_PRICE1K`. Tags can be used as a lookup key in `OpanAIWrapper.cost()` function to fix cost accounting for Azure Models with names that do not follow OpenAI model names. Yet it feels a bit of workaround/side-effect and breaking single-responsibility/separation of concerns. Long story short, tags solve the issues of arranging long config lists of models, yet they don't help with Azure Models mapping to OpenAI models. And it might be reasonable to revisit the whole idea of `OAI_PRICE1K` and openai_utils. E.g. look at few more scenarios: Azure models might get different prices at some point, metadata which now only includes costs might be extended with context window limits, there might be a more explicit way for the client code to define model costs/token limits in configs etc.

    openai_kwargs = set(inspect.getfullargspec(OpenAI.__init__).kwonlyargs)
    aopenai_kwargs = set(inspect.getfullargspec(AzureOpenAI.__init__).kwonlyargs)
    openai_kwargs = openai_kwargs & aopenai_kwargs
```

body:
I believe all current and future instances of `ConversableAgent` will have their `generate_reply` method using the logging middleware. This is because you are using the class's reference to the method. What you want to do is to use the object's local method instead.

@davorrunje Now I think about this a bit more, I think we want to make sure the effect of method rewriting to be local at each instance of agents. Perhaps we want to combine the `register_for_middleware` decorator with `add_middleware`. So, a user can simply do:

```python
agent_a = ConversableAgent()

add_middleware(agent_a.generate_reply, LoggingMiddleware())

# Now agent_a has logging capability.

agent_b = ConversableAgent()
# Agent b has no logging capability
```

Should be easy to do. We always make a new Middleware callable object using the input function. If the input function is not a Middleware callable, then we create a new one. If the input function is already a Middleware callable, then we also create a new one with combined middleware.

body: @LittleLittleCloud and @ekzhu you are absolutely right! We need to make middleware specific to an instance and not the class. Constructors should be used to set up the default middleware, but a user should be able to change the behaviour of each instance without affecting other objects.

body:
I'm concerned about the potential for user errors and system stability in that case. If users inadvertently forget the registration step, which could happen, it will result in the agents being partially initialized. This partial initialization could complicate the codebase (extra cognitive steps for client init), and we would need to consistently check for `None` clients, which not only adds complexity but also raises the risk of crashes if any check is overlooked.

State should either be:

- initialized all together by having the custom classes passed through the constructor of `Agent` to the constructor of `OpenAIWrapper` OR
- initialized in steps but completely, by using `register_client` and having it add to the `_client` list


what do you think?
author: olgavrou

body:
Agree with @olgavrou that having None in the client list during inference time causes instability and confusion, making the code more difficult to maintain. One thing we can do is to make sure the `config_list` and `clients` lists are in sync before inference and there is no None client. Also, if each config item in the confg list must be mapped to a client in a 1:1 mapping, then we should make the mapping explicit so someone reading the code immediately understand the design. 

I think initialization by passing the custom client class through the constructor of `Agent` makes harder for user to configure the `Agent`. Ideally, we would want to have a list of built-in clients to support most cases, so all they need to do is to pass in the `config_list` only. When they need to use custom client for special models, `register_client` explicitly is a good idea. Before inference, if we detect some config item in the `config_list` is not mapped to a client, then we raise.

As per our discussion offline. We have agreed to do the following:

1. `register_client` finds config items in the config list that matches `model` and append a client to the client list.
2. When `client.create` is called, we check everything in the config list has been mapped to an initialized client, if not then we raise an error.
3. If the user supplied a config list with an item that requires a custom client, they must call `agent.reigster_client` to activate the config item. 

This will lead to the same behavior as before for existing config lists, while requiring the `register_client` step for new config items.

# Create tasks for your agents
task1 = Task(

)

body:
Parameters after * must be passed as keyword arguments. In this case, there is a danger that the order of caller and executor is reversed by mistake and this is hard to detect since they both have the same type (e.g. type checking with mypy would not catch this). This syntax forces users to be explicit about what is the caller and what is the executor.

In general, it is typically used to make API extendable in future because it makes it easier to add new parameters. It is also used when there are too many parameters and it is easy to make a mistake by omitting one of them.

body:
I have been thinking perhaps we should make this method and the `process_last_message` private. They are not called directly from outside except as reference inside some capability classes. Having them public is quite confusing to user. It is also hard in case we want to refactor the implementation of the hooks in the future. 

We can expose a pre-defined set of "hookable points" in the `generate_reply` pipeline, e.g., as `Literal` types and register hooks given those types. For example, hookable points can be:
1. Process messages before entering the reply function pipeline.
2. Process messages after the reply function pipeline.

It is a good time to do this because I have not seen any code or anyone in the community making use of this hooks. So if a breaking change needs to be done then it's best to do it now. 

I think we should consider combining `process_last_message` and `process_all_messages`, and have an option when you register the hook choosing whether the hook is for the last message or all messages. That way we can mix different hooks without restriction ones before the others. 
 
@rickyloynd-microsoft
author: ekzhu

body:
Long-context handling is certainly related to memory, in the sense that context is a form of memory broadly speaking. But if we use the term memory in too many different settings, it will become less useful to us as a technical term. I suggest reserving _memory_ for information stored using vector databases, such as the memory used for teachable agents and the learning agents we are working on. I wouldn't use the term _RAG_ at all in these settings because that term implies too much about where the data comes from, like a set of files or the web.

In summary, I think _LongContext_ and _LongContextHandling_ are ideal descriptors of what this new capability is about.
author: rickyloynd-microsoft

body:
Yeah, private vs. public is a borderline case here. While they aren't called directly from the outside, hookable methods are definitely referenced from the outside in calls to `add_hook`. So I would leave them public, but make sure their doc strings point out that these hookable methods are not meant to be called directly, only passed to `add_hook`.

Combining `process_last_message `and `process_all_messages` _might_ reduce the total number of lines of code, but it would make the code much more complex, hard to read, and liable to break. It would also make the `add_hook` method considerably more complex to support the ability to disambiguate the intent (last message or all messages). Despite the similarity in their names, these two hookable methods have many differences. Their checked conditions are different, and their final steps are different (returning either the whole list, or a copy of it with only the last message modified). So I would keep them separate for now.

Regarding a pre-defined set of "hookable points", whether now is the time to do it or not, it should definitely be in a separate PR. I would like to discuss the architectural considerations leading to that PR.
author: rickyloynd-microsoft

Great discussion. 

My main concern is that having public methods that are only used as references exposes too large of a surface area for future maintenance and more work to understand the documentation. Thus adding `_` to the prefix of function names is a good idea. It makes it clear that these methods are not called from outside. 

We can use a static property of `Enum` type which can only be used as a reference, or, we can use `HookableMethod = Literal["pre_process_messages", "post_process_messages"]` to enforce the constraint on the input string. 

E.g., 
```python
# Define this somewhere, e.g., as a static property of `ConversableAgent`. 
HookableMethod` = Literal["pre_process_messages", "post_process_messages"]

# Public method for adding hooks.
def register_hook(handle: HookableMethod, hook: Callable):
  # we need validation on the hook function to make sure it is compatible with the handle
```

> introducing an extra concept (hook type)

We don't have to use a new name `hook_type`. I believe is only one concept and that is hookable method, which is the same what it means now. We could rename it to "hookable handle", which goes well with "hooks". But I don't have strong opinion on this. 

> There are many future capabilities we might want to add/hook that don't require a reply to be generated.

Right, so then we need to make these more digestible and a collection of hookable methods as literals could be explained together in the documentation for `register_hook`. If we leave them as public methods, then the doc is more "spread-out" and people have to jump around to find the meaning of each of the hookable method.

This is a great addition to the utils we have. My main question is do we want to use the same stream for all I/Os? 

The other things is the use of global stream object setting is something I am not very used to. How does it compare to setting the stream objects explicity in the methods that trigger I/Os?

--- Update ---

The office hour helps to clarify my questions. My answers are:

1. It is easy to use separate streams for different I/O purpose through the use of context manager. @davorrunje will document the usage of this scenario.
2. The default stream object is "thread-local" so there is no need to pass the stream object through constructors of different subclasses of `ConversableAgent`. The goal of this PR is to introduce the utility module for I/O and introduce `iostream.print` to replace built-in `print`. **For users not using the I/O utility module, there is no change in their code and the behavior remains the same.** For users of the new I/O utility module, they can customize where the data sent through `iostream.print` goes to, e.g., front-end.

body:
The default stream is not global, it is an instance of a [`ContextVar`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/contextvars.html). If you need to pass it down to every function down the call stack in your thread, you can just do this:
```python
with IOStream.set_default(iostream):
  some_code_calling_create_down_the_call_stack()
```

It will not affect other default streams in other threads/async call stacks. In servers, that's IMO the easiest way to support multiple input/output streams.

This function is calculating tokens by splitting words, which is different than how token_count_utils.count_token() works. This means that the two methods might have slightly different values. This if statement is an extra guard to make sure that the simplistic calculation will never be larger than token_count_utils.count_token. If its slightly smaller, I'm ok with that since its below the max threshold.

body:
There're several strategies that can be applied here
- invoke immediately and return result only: this strategy makes the function_call invisible to other agents and makes the most compatibility
- invoke immediately and return [function_call, function_call_result], similar to have user proxy agent execute function, but only require one agent to complete
- return function_call object only: the common two agent chat pattern

The current implementation is if `function_map` is provided, the first strategy will be applied, and if not, the third strategy will be applied.

body:
In lines 209-211, there's a potential code path where the condition `if self.agents[(offset + i) % len(self.agents)] in agents` never evaluates to `True`. This scenario would lead the function to implicitly return `None`, which is not an intended outcome and causes type checking tools like mypy to raise concerns. This specific situation arises when there is no intersection between the lists `self.agents` and `agents`, meaning there's no valid "next agent" to return.

To address this issue, I introduced an `UndefinedNextAgent` exception raise earlier in the code (before reaching the problematic section) if it's determined that there's no intersection between `self.agents` and the provided `agents` list. This preemptive check ensures that the function either successfully finds and returns the next agent or explicitly fails by raising an exception, thereby eliminating the implicit `None` return path.

However, mypy (or similar static analysis tools) may still raise an error because it cannot infer that this preemptive check guarantees the condition in lines 209-211 will always find a match. The tool's static analysis does not trace the logical implications of the intersection check to understand that the later loop's condition is guaranteed to succeed at least once if the code execution reaches that point.

I simplified the code a little bit as well to be explicit with what the intent of the function should be, let me know what you think of the following:

```python
def next_agent(self, agent: Agent, agents: Optional[List[Agent]] = None) -> Agent:
        """Return the next agent in the list."""
        agents = agents or self.agents

        # Ensure the provided list of agents is a subset of self.agents
        if not set(agents).issubset(set(self.agents)):
            raise UndefinedNextAgent()

        # Try to find the index of the current agent in the provided list
        idx = self.agents.index(agent) if agent in self.agents else -1

        for i in range(1, len(self.agents) + 1):
            next_agent = self.agents[(idx + i) % len(self.agents)]
            if next_agent in agents:
                return next_agent

        raise UndefinedNextAgent()
```

@staticmethod
def simple_nested_chat(

body:
I might suggest the following:
```
def register_nested_chats(
    self,
    trigger: Union[Type['Agent'], str, 'Agent', Callable[['Agent'], bool], List],
    chat_queue: List[Dict[str, Any]],
    reply_func_from_nested_chat: Union[Callable, str] = "auto",
    position: int = 2,
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> None:
    """
    Register a nested chat reply function to handle specific triggers.
    
    This method allows registering a custom or predefined function that initiates nested chats based on specific triggers. It is a higher-order function that wraps the reply function for nested chats, allowing it to be registered with additional context like `chat_queue` and other configurations.
    
    Args:
        trigger: The condition that triggers the nested chat reply function. It can be an Agent class, string (name of the agent), Agent instance, a callable that returns a boolean, or a list of these types.
        chat_queue: A list of dictionaries, each representing a chat object with specific configurations for initiating a nested chat.
        reply_func_from_nested_chat: A callable or the string 'auto' to determine the reply function used for the nested chats. If 'auto', a predefined function is used. The function should follow the signature:
            ```python
            def reply_func_from_nested_chat(
                chat_queue: List[Dict],
                recipient: 'ConversableAgent',
                messages: Optional[List[Dict]] = None,
                sender: Optional['Agent'] = None,
                config: Optional[Any] = None,
            ) -> Tuple[bool, Union[str, Dict, None]]:
            ```
        position: The order in which this nested chat reply function is considered relative to other reply functions. A lower number means higher priority.
        kwargs: Additional keyword arguments forwarded to the `register_reply` method, which can include configurations specific to the nested chat.
    
    Returns:
        None: This function does not return a value but registers a reply function based on the provided parameters.
    
    Raises:
        AssertionError: If `reply_func_from_nested_chat` is not callable.
    """
```

body:
What do you think about throwing a warning over here? 

As far as I have seen, this is common pattern that we need to have it in each synchronous/async hook to check if the registered method matches the expected execution context, ensuring that asynchronous hooks are not mistakenly used in synchronous contexts and vice versa.

Can we have a more generalized logic to control such misplacements? 

What do you think about updating the `register_hook` method a bit to support this?

```py
    def register_hook(self, hookable_method: Callable, hook: Callable):
        """
        Registers a hook to be called by a hookable method, in order to add a capability to the agent.
        Registered hooks are kept in lists (one per hookable method), and are called in their order of registration.

        Args:
            hookable_method: A hookable method implemented by ConversableAgent.
            hook: A method implemented by a subclass of AgentCapability.
        """
        assert hookable_method in self.hook_lists, f"{hookable_method} is not a hookable method."
        hook_list = self.hook_lists[hookable_method]
        assert hook not in hook_list, f"{hook} is already registered as a hook."

        
        #### SUGGESTED CHANGES STARTS ####
        expected_async = hookable_method.startswith('a_')
        hook_is_async = inspect.iscoroutinefunction(hook)
        if expected_async != hook_is_async:
            context_type = "asynchronous" if expected_async else "synchronous"
            warnings.warn(f"Hook '{hook.__name__}' is {'asynchronous' if hook_is_async else 'synchronous'}, "
                f"but it's being registered in a {context_type} context ('{hookable_method}'). "
                "Ensure the hook matches the expected execution context.", UserWarning)
        #### SUGGESTED CHANGES ENDS ####


        hook_list.append(hook)
```

This suggested solution above, can also address the suggestion from @gagb https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/1845/files#r1518417767.

body:
1. Can you add a docstring there?
2. The function looks good based on LMM's current features. However, if there are several non-text elements in the `message`, then the order would be wrong. How about:

```python
if not context.get("carryover"):
    return message  # Make sure no ordering issues.

prefix_msg = {"type": "text", "text": ""}
index_to_split = 0  # To keep track of where to split the messages

# Iterate over message to concatenate text messages and find split index
for index, msg in enumerate(message):
    if msg.get("type") == "text":
        prefix_msg["text"] += msg["text"] + "\n"
        index_to_split = index + 1  # Update the index to split since this is a text message
    else:
        break  # Stop at the first non-text message

remaining_message = message[index_to_split:]

# Process the concatenated text message
prefix_msg["text"] = self._process_carryover(prefix_msg["text"], context)

# Reconstruct the message, starting with the processed text message if not empty
reconstructed_message = [prefix_msg] + remaining_message if prefix_msg["text"].strip() else remaining_message

return reconstructed_message
```

With this update, if the first element is an image, then the carryover will be in the front of the image.

body:
To have a better separation of concerns, I split the functions into two:
```python
def _process_multimodal_carryover(self, message: List, kwargs: dict) -> List[Dict]:
        """Adds context to the multimodal text message."""
        if not context.get("carryover"):
            return message
        
        found_text = False
        for msg in message:
            if msg.get("type") == "text":
                msg["text"] = self._process_carryover(msg["text"], kwargs)
                found_text = True
                break

        if not found_text:
            message.append({"type": "text", "text": self._process_carryover("", kwargs)})
        return message
```
```python
def _prepare_multimodal_message(self, message: List) -> List[Dict]:
        """Handles cases when the message contents contains mutliple of the text types.

        Merges the text messages into a single text message.
        """
        reconstructed_messages = [{"type": "text", "text": ""}]
        found_text = False
        first_text_idx = -1
        for msg in message:
            if msg.get("type") == "text":
                reconstructed_messages[0]["text"] += msg["text"] + "\n"
                if not found_text:
                    found_text = True
                    first_text_idx += 1
            else:
                reconstructed_messages.append(copy.deepcopy(msg))

        # Delete the text message if it is empty
        if reconstructed_messages[0]["text"] == "":
            del reconstructed_messages[0]

        if first_text_idx != -1:
            # Move the text message to the appropriate idx to maintain the order
            reconstructed_messages.insert(first_text_idx, reconstructed_messages.pop(0))

        return reconstructed_messages
```

Let me know what you think of this approach

```python
def _process_multimodal_carryover(self, message: List, kwargs: dict) -> List[Dict]:
        """Adds context to the multimodal text message."""
        if not context.get("carryover"):
            return message
        
        return [{"type": "text", "text": self._process_carryover("", kwargs)}] + message
```

In this case, we don't modify any order of the message components, and we only put the "carryover" into the front (by the definition of carryover). It is ok to have 2 text components in the front of the message.

Hey @AaronWard, glad you noticed the PR. One thing I'd like to confirm is whether your intent is to avoid unrunnable errors when environment variables are not set.

If I understand correctly, the intent of using `os.getenv(base_url, default=base_url)` is to allow the person writing the code to pass values in directly using the parameter `model_api_key_map` in the absence of an `.env` file.

No doubt this is a great idea: even if I don't have the `.env` file set up, I can run it fine. 
However, this I think may be contrary to the original intent of setting up `.env`, as I precisely don't want to expose my api_key directly in the code, and the [doc](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/notebook/config_loader_utility_functions.ipynb) also mentions data privacy as follows:
```
The provided utility functions assist users in managing these configurations effectively. 
Ensure your API keys and other sensitive data are stored securely. 
You might store keys in .txt or .env files or environment variables for local development. 
Never expose your API keys publicly.
```
So personally, I think this may not be ideal.

---

In general, I think the code will work fine with or without assigning values to the parameter `default`, the difference is whether those parameters are set to `None` or to the values in `model_api_key_map`, depending on your purpose.

If you think `os.getenv(base_url, default=base_url)` is better, then I will modify my PR. thanks again for your reply.

Actually the intent would be to allow users to asssign values to the other parameters in `model_api_key_map` (besides `api_key_env_var `) via a `.env` file rather than passing them as strings. 

The suggestion would allow people to define them programatically, for example
```python
...
"gpt-3.5-turbo": {
    "api_key_env_var": "ANOTHER_API_KEY",
    "api_type": "aoai",
    "api_version": "v2",
    "base_url": "https://api.someotherapi.com",
},
```
or in your case, access them in `.env` (assuming you have these in your `.env` file) :
```python
"gpt-3.5-turbo": {
    "api_key_env_var": "ANOTHER_API_KEY",
    "api_type": "API_TYPE",
    "api_version": "API_VERSION",
    "base_url": "API_OAI_ENDPOINT",
},
```

For example, if "v2" isn't available as an enviroment variable, adding the default would allow the string representation to be used - accommodating for both scenarios.

You raise a good point. My aim was to address scenarios like an agent joining a group chat midway, where it's crucial for the agent to grasp the full conversation context. Compressing only the latest message might not be sufficient. `TransformMessages` capability hooks to `process_all_messages_before_reply`.

author: WaelKarkoub

body:
> You raise a good point. My aim was to address scenarios like an agent joining a group chat midway, where it's crucial for the agent to grasp the full conversation context. Compressing only the latest message might not be sufficient. `TransformMessages` capability hooks to `process_all_messages_before_reply`. This ensures that information loss is minimized and mainly impacts agents that have this transform applied (or any other transform like token truncation). Let me know what you think.

I agree that it is a useful functionality. One thought that I have is including another method to the `MessageTransform`'s protocol, something like `init_apply_transform`, that could include the transformation that should be applied when a new agent is initialized (if this is not applied for a transformation, it could be simply passed). This way the different functionalities would be decoupled (and possibly it could be useful for future transformations also).



> In terms of latency performance, I'm letting the user decide what trade-offs to make.

Of course, what I mean is that if the user by accident sets the `messages_to_compress` to *all* it would lead to considerable delays, especially as the number of messages increases, and it would lead to a bug difficult to identify.

Let me know your thoughts on these, and I would also be happy to collaborate with you.
author: giorgossideris

body: I like the `init_apply_transform` idea, what do you think of just adding this flag to `TextMessageCompressor` instead of `MessageTransform`? The idea behind `MessageTransform` is to keep it as simple as possible to implement, and only add methods that are common between all transforms. `init_apply_transform` wouldn't make sense as not all the transforms require to be initialized (e.g. `MessageHistoryLimiter`)
author: WaelKarkoub

body:
Not certain if this is an optimal solution for several reasons:

* This specific initialization might also be necessary for future transformations, not just limited to `TextMessageCompressor`.
* With the current implementation, to apply the `TextMessageCompressor` transformation to a newly created agent, you need to instantiate two `TextMessageCompressor` objects: one to apply the transformation to all available messages and another to apply it to each new message. This implementation could be improved.
* Opting for `init_apply_transform`, it becomes effortless to simply `pass` it for transformations it doesn't apply.
author: giorgossideris

1. To simplify the constructor,

body:
Using an underscore `_` before a variable name indicates that it is a temporary or unimportant variable, serving the purpose of readability. They are not considered private member variables in this context because they are not prefixed with `self.`

"Use one leading underscore only for non-public methods and instance variables," as stated in [PEP 8](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/#function-and-variable-names). In this case, it is more of a personal convention.

We've dbs like `chroma`, `qdrant`, etc. One product would like to have only one of these dbs. Say `chroma`. Now, in my product, a chatbot, I use chromadb as the `VectorDB`. Just an update that I realised that I wasn't using the `role_for_select_speaker_mesasges` so I have updated my code to use that role.

An important note is that as we are not adding the message directly now and are depending on existing functions to create the message with our user-defined role, I have added an attribute to the starting message called `override_role`:
```
        # Run the speaker selection chat
        result = checking_agent.initiate_chat(
            speaker_selection_agent,
            cache=None,  # don't use caching for the speaker selection chat
            message={'content':self.select_speaker_prompt(agents),'override_role':self.role_for_select_speaker_messages},
            max_turns=2
            * max(1, max_attempts),  # Limiting the chat to the number of attempts, including the initial one
            clear_history=False,
            silent=not self.select_speaker_auto_verbose,  # Base silence on the verbose attribute
        )
```

and this is used in ConversableAgent's `_append_oai_message`:
```

body:
Oops, I completely overlooked this PR. Tomorrow, I’ll demonstrate the initial issue I encountered, which aligns closely with @patrickwasp’s observation:

When launching a code executor from within a Docker container (primary), relying solely on the work_dir argument assumes that the newly spawned container (sibling) shares the same absolute path as the host system, which isn’t the case for most scenarios.

Introducing the new bind_dir prop grants us the ability to spawn a new container (sibling) from within the app container (primary), binding its working directory to a specified HOST directory. This allows us to maintain internal operations within the primary container’s working directory, which can be linked to the primary by sharing the same HOST directory, rather than requiring identical container/host paths.

@jackgerrits Thanks for your comment.

Regarding this, I retained the `Optional[str]` because this field is not mandatory; users have the choice to either include or omit this field.

If we decide that the `Optional` annotation should be eliminated, it would be consistent to also reevaluate the use of `Optional` on [line#37](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/2321/files#diff-bb64e2cb33935f6ae71ffa200d71aa39ec2de8908ede9d21aede7f8408cadc95R37).

To further illustrate my point, let's look at an example with `pydantic`: to allow a field to accept either a variable or use a default value, we would define it as follows:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Optional

class SimpleTextBrowser(BaseModel):
    bing_base_url: Optional[str] = Field(default="https://api.bing.microsoft.com/v7.0/search")

# then we can call it by
if __name__ == "__main__":
    option1 = SimpleTextBrowser()  # Option 1
    option2 = SimpleTextBrowser(bing_base_url="https://mlop-azure-gateway.mediatek.inc/v7.0/search")  # Option 2
    print(option1)
    # >> output: bing_base_url='https://api.bing.microsoft.com/v7.0/search'
    print(option2)
    # >> output: bing_base_url='https://mlop-azure-gateway.mediatek.inc/v7.0/search'
```

For this reason, I think keeping this `Optional` is necessary, which makes code more clear; it works even if I remove `Optional`, but it will be unclear.

Why version 1.x of pydantic? It will stop being supported even for security bugs very soon, see https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/version-policy/#pydantic-v1

### Pydantic V1

Active development of V1 has already stopped, however critical bug fixes and security vulnerabilities will be fixed in V1 for one year after the release of V2 (June 30, 2024).

We should also limit version ranges of other packages, e.g.
```suggestion
        "gemini": ["google-generativeai>=0.5,<1", "pillow", "pydantic==1.10.9"],
```
The new major version will surely break everything and we should make sure that it doesn't get installed at some future point.

Sorry for bringing this up again, but I have another suggestion. There are two potential issues with this approach:
1. In case of import error, the actual error is never propagated to a user
2. Double definition of `GeminiClient` will generate a large number of warnings for type checker.

Alternatively, you could save import exception and make the test here. Something like:
```python
try:
    from autogen.oai.gemini import GeminiClient
    gemini_import_exception: Optional[ImportError] = None
except ImportError as e:
    gemini_import_exception = e
```
and then later you can use `raise from gemini_import_exception`:
```python
if gemini_import_exception:
    raise ImportError("Please install `google-generativeai` to use Google OpenAI API.") from gemini_import_exception
```

```
def _chat_history_to_openai(self, chat_history: list) -> list:
        """
            takes the chat history as produced by prompt flow and formats it for use in the simulator
            promptflow uses the following format:
                chat_history = [{"inputs":{"question":"What did OpenAI announce on March 2023?"},
                                 "outputs":{"answer":"On March 2023, OpenAI announced the release of GPT-4"}}]
            simulator uses the following format used by openai chat models:
                [{"role": "human", "content": "What did OpenAI announce on March 2023?"}, 
                 {"role": "agent", "content": "On March 2023, OpenAI announced the release of GPT-4"}]
        """
        formatted_chat_history = []
        for i in chat_history:
            formatted_chat_history.append({"role": "user", "content": i["inputs"][self.question]})
            formatted_chat_history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": i["outputs"][self.answer]})
        return formatted_chat_history
```

```
def _chat_history_to_pf(self, chat_history: list) -> list:
        """
            takes the chat history as produced by openai and converts it to the prompt flow and format
            simulator uses the following format used by openai chat models:
                [{"role": "user", "content": "What did OpenAI announce on March 2023?"}, 
                 {"role": "assistant", "content": "On March 2023, OpenAI announced the release of GPT-4"}]
            promptflow uses the following format:
                chat_history = [{"inputs":{"question":"What did OpenAI announce on March 2023?"},
                                 "outputs":{"answer":"On March 2023, OpenAI announced the release of GPT-4", "context":"some context for the prior answer"}}]
        """
        chat_history = chat_history.copy()
        # filter out any messages that are not from the user or assistant
        chat_history = [message for message in chat_history if message["role"] in ["user", "assistant"]]
        pf_chat_history = []
        for i in range(0, len(chat_history)-1, 2):
            pf_chat_history.append({"inputs":{self.question: chat_history[i]["content"]},
                                    "outputs":{self.answer: chat_history[i+1]["content"]}})
        return pf_chat_history
```

    def _check_tokens_threshold(self, messages: List[Dict]) -> bool:
        """Returns True if the total number of tokens in the messages is greater than or equal to the `min_theshold_tokens`."""
        if not self._min_tokens:
            return False
            
        messages_tokens = sum(_count_tokens(msg["content"]) for msg in messages if "content" in msg)
        return messages_tokens >= self._min_threshold_tokens
```

body:
It wraps the __init__ function of the class to assign an agentops ID. Then in our instrumentation of LLM calls, we look up the call stack to see if the call or `Event` is being made by a decorated agent class. If so, we relate them in our db

```python
original_init = obj.__init__

            def new_init(self, *args, **kwargs):
                try:
                    original_init(self, *args, **kwargs)
                    self.agent_ops_agent_id = str(uuid4())
                    Client().create_agent(self.agent_ops_agent_id, self.agent_ops_agent_name)
                except AttributeError as e:
                    logger.warning("AgentOps failed to track an agent. This often happens if agentops.init() was not "
                                  "called before initializing an agent with the @track_agent decorator.")
                    raise e

            obj.__init__ = new_init
```

body:
`resume_chat` is interesting though it is adding a new API method that is in parallel with `initiate_chat`. We can decouple "resume" from "chat", so we offer more flexibility. For example:

```python
messages = load_history() # some user-defined code to load historical messages

# Resume to a state of group chat specified by the message history and other
# arguments similar to the `resume_chat` you have, except the summary method and args. 
group_chat_manager.resume(messages=messages, ...)

# New the group chat is in a pre-configured state, start a new conversation with it
result = admin.initiate_chat(group_chat_manager, message="a new message to the group chat", summary_method="reflection_with_llm")
```

Generally, we can think of the `resume` method as a `pre-configuration` step for group chat -- it can be used to reload a previous chat, but user can also provide custom message history for different purposes (e.g., summarized chunks of messages, contextual information to be shared with all participants, etc.).

Some good points raised above. When I implemented the agent-based select speaker, I didn't consider the need to use a different configuration, hence the inclusion of the selector, which seemed like a logical place to get the config.

The `selector`, for the purposes of "auto" select speaker mode, is just to get the `llm_config` from the group chat manager. So, having a separate `llm_config` attribute on GroupChat that is clearly for the purpose of the "auto" select speaker agent chat would, I agree, make it simpler for a developer to understand.

Now, having said that...

> Then, an alternative is to avoid creating a new `speaker_selection_agent` every time, but simply reuse the `selector` as the `speaker_selection_agent`. Then we don't need to worry about the client class registration in `GroupChat`.
> @marklysze what do you think?

For example, the GroupChatManager has `run_chat` in the reply register, so would this be called during the select speaker agent-to-agent chat?

body:
Originally I used `self._silent` but this test failed: `test/agentchat/test_groupchat.py:277` 

Specifically:
```
    groupchat = autogen.GroupChat(agents=[agent1, agent2], messages=[], max_round=2)
    group_chat_manager = autogen.ConversableAgent(name="deputy_manager", llm_config=False)
    group_chat_manager.register_reply(
        autogen.Agent,
        reply_func=autogen.GroupChatManager.run_chat,
        config=groupchat,
        reset_config=autogen.GroupChat.reset,
    )
    agent1.initiate_chat(group_chat_manager, message="hello")
```

Since the group_chat_manager is a `ConversableAgent` and not a `GroupChatManager`, it did not have the `_silent` attribute available. Instead of attempting or requesting a deeper refactor to include this value, especially in the edge case of supporting a "plugin" version of the group chat manager, I took this approach.

----
This decision reflected in one of the PR notes for reference:
- GroupChat silent configuration tweaked to support the plugin use case without adding additional vars to ConversableAgent.

        if WIN32:

I think these changes are important, but I have a couple of thoughts:
1. `process_last_received_message` passes in just the content to the registered hook method, so it must be a content type (I'm planning to open a PR to define that, but here it is `MessageContentType = Union[str, List[Union[Dict, str]]]`)

body:
I have thought about this a bit, for robustness and from a developer who wants to use AutoGen in a production scenario, I think it's important to manage types and values. I feel that letting things fail isn't an ideal experience. Temperature is fairly straightforward, yes, but others are more nuanced in their type and ranges. I'm working on a Together client and that has more parameters and some have specific ranges (-2...2).

For the smaller models, for which Mistral and Together will allow, to make them work effectively it is likely developers will need to tweak these parameters. The models aren't as flexible as OpenAI's. 

If we can make it more robust, less likely to break on a developer, it seems better to me.

@Git-Noob123 thank you for the notebook! 

I like this notebook since it's a good example to show how `process_message_before_send` (hooks in general) works. 

If we hook `TransformMessages` onto `process_message_before_send` it makes debugging these agents much more difficult, since you don't know the ground truth (as it gets modified before being stored in the context history).  And as you may already know, it's already difficult to debug vanilla LLMs without any modifications.

In the intro, we should maybe explain the differences between each hookable method, and why you picked the `process_message_before_send`

body:
Atlas Vector Search assigns a score, in a fixed range from 0 to 1 only, to every document that it returns. For cosine and dotProduct [similarities](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-search/field-types/knn-vector/#std-label-fts-knn-vector-type-options), Atlas Vector Search normalizes the score using the following algorithm:

score = (1 + cosine/dot_product(v1,v2)) / 2

The vector score is already essentially vector distance, normalized between 0 and 1. 

What do you think is the best path forward here @thinkall ?
I changed the implementation to be:
```
pipeline.append({"$match": {"score": {"lte": distance_threshold}}})
```

instead of:
```
pipeline.append({"$match": {"score": {"gte": distance_threshold}}})
```
author: ranfysvalle02

body: In the signature, it's better to keep the same meaning of `distance_threshold` accross different vectordbs. In mongodb, I'd suggest you create an internal variable `similarity_threshold = 1 - distance_threshold`, and  do `pipeline.append({"$match": {"score": {"gte": similarity_threshold}}})`

TextMessage("What's the weather in seattle", from: user)

### Explanation of VerifierAgent's Role

VerifierAgent ensures the criteria used to evaluate a utility are effective for the end-user, maintaining both robustness and high discriminative power. It does this through two main actions:

1. **Criteria Stability**: 
   - Ensures criteria are essential, non-redundant, and consistently measurable.
   - Iterates over generating and quantifying criteria, eliminating redundancies, and evaluating their stability.
   - Retains only the most robust criteria.

2. **Discriminative Power**: 
   - Tests the system's reliability by introducing adversarial examples (noisy or compromised data).
   - Assesses the system's ability to distinguish these from standard cases.
   - If the system fails, it indicates the need for better criteria to handle varied conditions effectively.

body:
Hi, thank you for developing this!
Quick question. Since you're leveraging the Groq client anyway, would it make sense to inherit it? 

```
class GroqClient(Groq):

    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        Groq.__init__(self)
        """Requires api_key or environment variable to be set"""
```
Then, to get the response you use the client's create method (`self.chat.completion.create(**groq_params)`)

Also, if my memory serves me right, the Groq client might have built-in retries you can leverage. 
I believe the property name is `retry` and you can set the `max_attempts`, and `wait`. It saves you from using the while loop :)

Thoughts?
author: Gal-Gilor

body:
Thanks for your feedback @Gal-Gilor!

A question on inheriting - I assume that will bring forward all the Groq functions and attributes, I'm not sure if this will conflict with the class as is (or anything that AutoGen expects client classes to have in the future). Am I right in that thinking?

Re the retries - oh, I see `max_retries`. I also can see that they retry by default. I agree it would be handy not to have the loop. I'll test that out and perhaps set it as 5 to replace the loop code. Thanks!

body:
Legacy `generate_code_execution_reply` had this function with `logs`. So I think it should be default behavior. To be honest I think it may be possibly be over-engineering to add it to `code_execution_config`. There aren't other configurations for controlling logging visibility in the project that I've found. I don't know if it would be all that intuitive of a property. What do you think about keeping it simpler? If you'd still want it, I'd make the prop `hide_code_file_output`, which feels out of place alongside `use_docker`, `work_dir`, `timeout` and `last_n_messages`. 
Also think it's unlikely it'd break any app regexing the output. Broken regex would look something like `exitcode: (.*)\nCode Output (.*)`, which would look for multiple capturing groups at once.
 If that's a concern I think there could also be a conversation about a different data structure than the brittleness of a string to support api consistency (such as a metadata output property alongside `content`).

async def (_a)_summary_from_nested_chats(...):

    res = await a_initiate_chats(chat_to_run)
    index_of_last_chat = chat_to_run[-1]["chat_id"]

body:
@marklysze I marked the PR as a draft as I am not sure yet what kind of workaround is the best one. The issue seems to be on the OpenAPI side and it is more common with GPT-4o-mini than older models. Maybe we should remove names only if we get an exception? Even changing the system message a little bit helps sometimes. The list of possible workarounds is (https://community.openai.com/t/bizarre-issue-preventing-response-from-gpt-4o-mini-the-model-produces-invalid-content/875432):

- Remove tools and tool_choice args.
- Slightly reduce the length of the prompt, even by a couple of words.
- Add at least a second user message or an assistant message.
- Change the name or remove the name parameter (but that didn’t always work, depending on the prompt). Some names work, others don’t. ‘Gregory’ worked, for example.
- Change the message. Some work and some don’t. ‘Hello.’ didn’t work, but ‘Hello, friend.’ worked.
- Change to gpt-4o or gpt-3.5-turbo.
author: davorrunje

async def get_user_input(self, user_prompt: Dict, timeout: int, websocket: WebSocket) -> str:

                    await self.disconnect(websocket)

body:
Seems like there are two separate output streams here, perhaps it deserves to be two separate log handler classes instead of one? We can add them both by default, or just the console one by default, and have user add it when needed. 

```python
import logging
from autogen_agentchat.logging import EVENT_LOGGER_NAME, FileLogHandler

logger = logging.getLogger(EVENT_LOGGER_NAME)
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
logger.addHandler(FileLogHandler(filename="..."))
```

or, assuming we have both handlers on by default, and user doesn't have to do anything to get both console and file logs. But if they want to customize anything: 

```python
import logging
from autogen_agentchat.logging import EVENT_LOGGER_NAME

logger = logging.getLogger(EVENT_LOGGER_NAME)
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
logger.addHandler(...) # some user-defined logger here. 
```

body:
Several good additions here.
Some thoughts on potential improvements for consideration:

- IMO The teams page would really help users by  providing guidance on all of the supported team presets. This could be the place where the reader comes to learn of what presets exist and which one to use. The current organization instead introduces single agent teams and two agent teams which are not actual team types.  This could be confusing. 
Also, as we add more team types, the teams page could be a a natural place to add them .. RoundRobin, Selector/LLM, MagenticOne.

- I really like the idea of mentioning support for single or multiple agents in a team.  IMO The idea of single or double or triple or n-agent teams is more of a parameter/implementation detail rather than an high level concept.   The way it is currently written (as headings) sounds like a Single Agent Team is a _type_ of team. In reality it is a RoundRobingGroupChat (or could be any team type .. ) with only one agent. This concept will be perhaps better served by introducing the RoundRobinGroupChat, and mentioning it can one or n number of agents and schedule them to speak in round robin fashion.

Suggestions on organizing the teams page:

- Teams
   -  Add a section or even a list of cards highlighting current supported teams . Perhaps right afeter the diagram .. a list with links to roundrobin, selector,
   - Change .. A Single Agent Team -> RoundRobinGroupChat 
      - Mention that a team can take only a single agent or a list of agents and show the examples.  I really like the reflection reference! 
      
      
It might still be a good idea to discuss all team types in the teams page (would be a long page, but could be the single location where we disucss all team types, some maintenance benefits there). 
Swarm is more of a detail or concept with a team. These could be organized into a Team Concepts section on same page. A list of concepts

- **Participants** a team can have one or more participants. This can be useful for patterns e.g. reflection
- **Run/Run_stream**: teams have a run and run stream method.      
- **Reset/Resume**. teams  can be reset (resets termination)  resumed (by calling run .. and assumes the agents are held in memory) 
- ***Handoff** teams implement a handoff pattern by sending a handoff message ...

Thanks! 

We can have two examples:

One chatbot scenario, such as the flight example but with more realistic user experience, with more options such as flight search, cancellation, rebooking, status, etc. Use relevant tools with preset outputs. For the chat bot scenario, it is important to constantly engage the user, so you want to set `max_turn=1` in `Swarm` to make sure it is returning the control back to the user each time an agent responds. You don't need to include handoff to the user because `max_turn=1`. Also, we can show that a handoff can be customized with a `autogen_agentchat.agents.HandOff` class. 

For max_turn let's wait for this one: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/4143

The second example is more autonomous. I would go with content generation such as investment/market research. No need to be super fancy just use tools with preset outputs. The planner agent hands off to all other agents, while all other agents hand off back to the planner agent. 

I use draw.io to create SVGs for visualizations. I think we should have a visualization for both scenarios. You can save the drawio source in the `python/packages/autogen-core/docs/drawio` folder. Then I produce SVG by exporting and choose selection only and auto light mode. Don't set `transparent background` because it is going to mess up the dark mode. body:
Hi @ekzhu 
For the first example, after testing `Swarm` with `max_turns=1` as suggested, I don’t think this would work as expected.

```python
travel_team = Swarm(
    participants=[travel_agent, flights_refunder],
    termination_condition=TextMentionTermination("TERMINATE"),
    max_turns=1,
)

user_input = "Help me refund my flight."

while True:
    result = await travel_team.run(task=user_input)
    last_message = result.messages[-1]
    print(f"{last_message.source}: {last_message.content}")
    
    if isinstance(last_message, TaskResult) and last_message.stop_reason == "TERMINATE":
        break

    user_input = input("\nUser: ")
```

With something like the above, every time we stop the `travel_team` because of `max_turns`, the user inputs something. This user message would be `message_thread[-1]`, the `SwarmGroupChatManager` selects the next speaker if the last message in `message_thread` is a handoff message. Hence if the last message is a handoff between travel_agent to flights_refunder, this handoff message would be lost and the next speaker would be `travel_agent` again.

Am I missing something?
author: gziz
